metadata.title: AI advocates and cautious critics: How AI attitudes, AI interest, use of AI, and AI literacy build university students' AI self-efficacy

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study recruited university students via the Prolific platform from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Germany (N=1465 after exclusions). The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights or any sampling/replicate-weight variables, and the analysis is based on a non-representative convenience sample rather than an ILSA-style probability sample. Because no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate design (BRR/jackknife) is mentioned, student_weights_used and replicate_weights_used are left as null. The data preparation described includes excluding invalid attention-check failures, removing respondents who did not finish the survey, and excluding very fast completions (<5 minutes), followed by IRT-based scoring and z-standardization for the clustering step.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; instead, it measures AI self-efficacy, AI literacy (via an IRT scoring model), AI interest, AI attitudes, and AI use using survey items. Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scores, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-item or missing-response handling procedure (e.g., imputation or deletion rules), so missing-data handling is a reporting gap rather than a design feature.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were recruited in December 2023 via Prolific from the US, UK, and Germany. From 1558 initial participants, the authors excluded 93 invalid cases: 14 failed both attention checks, 75 did not finish the survey, and 3 completed the survey too quickly (less than 5 minutes; Mdn=19.1), leaving an analytic sample of N=1465 (NUS=494, NUK=499, NGER=472).

main_findings.dataset_used: Cross-national university student survey (US, UK, Germany; December 2023 recruitment)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path analysis: Use of AI → AI interest: 0.434 (p < .01); Positive attitudes toward AI → AI interest: 0.618 (p-significant as reported); Negative attitudes toward AI → AI interest: −0.057 (p = .12, non-significant). Correlations: AI interest with positive attitudes: 0.65***; with use of AI: 0.56***. Additional analysis (AI self-efficacy): Path analysis (SEM path model): AI literacy → AI self-efficacy: 0.144 (p < .01); AI interest → AI self-efficacy: 0.245 (p < .01). Direct effects of positive/negative attitudes and use on AI self-efficacy were non-significant. Additional analysis (Student group membership (AI Advocates / Cautious Critics / Pragmatic Observers)): Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) selected three components using BIC/ABIC/AIC/CAIC; group sizes: AI Advocates 703/1465 (47.99%), Cautious Critics 305/1465 (20.82%), Pragmatic Observers 457/1465 (31.19%). MANOVA (Pillai’s trace): F = 53.44 (p < .01), Pillai’s trace = 0.180.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using cross-national university student survey data from the US, UK, and Germany, the study leveraged AI use and AI attitudes to predict AI interest, finding that AI use and positive attitudes toward AI were strong positive predictors of AI interest while negative attitudes had only a marginal, non-significant relationship. This indicates that AI education programs should prioritize hands-on AI interaction and foster positive, engagement-supporting attitudes to increase AI interest, while treating negative attitudes as something that may require targeted instructional design rather than assuming they automatically suppress interest.

data.outcome_summary: The study recruited university students from the United States (n=494), the United Kingdom (n=499), and Germany (n=472) via Prolific and analyzed N=1465 after excluding attention-check failures, non-completers, and very fast responders. It used IRT scoring for AI literacy and then applied path analysis (SEM) to test relationships among AI use, AI interest, AI attitudes, AI literacy, and AI self-efficacy, reporting strong model fit across the total sample and country subsamples (e.g., total-sample χ²=3.102, p=.999; CFI=1.005; RMSEA=0.000). Key effects were AI use → AI interest (0.434, p<.01) and AI interest → AI self-efficacy (0.245, p<.01), with AI literacy also contributing modestly (0.144, p<.01). The authors also identified three student groups (AI Advocates, Cautious Critics, Pragmatic Observers) using Gaussian mixture modeling and found significant group differences (MANOVA Pillai’s trace=0.180, p<.01). Limitations include cross-sectional, non-representative sampling and no reported missing-data handling strategy.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper uses Gaussian Mixture Models for profiling and path analysis for relationships, it does not train predictive ML models with supervised targets, and it does not report any ML algorithm performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) for prediction. Therefore, ml_techniques.primary is left null and all_techniques is empty to avoid misclassifying GMM/SEM/IRT as ML predictive modeling. The extraction focuses on the empirical statistical findings rather than ML prediction.
